title: Six Dead in Indiana as Historic Flooding Triggers Federal Emergency Declaration
excerpt: President Trump has approved an emergency declaration for more than 50 Indiana counties after storms and flooding killed at least six people, displaced hundreds and left nearly one million without power.
body:
• At least six people have died in Indiana after a week of severe storms and flooding, including a 4-year-old boy, with deaths reported across five counties.
  • President Trump approved an emergency declaration covering more than 50 Indiana counties, unlocking FEMA aid to cover 75% of eligible emergency response costs.
  • More than 400 residents have been evacuated in Indianapolis neighborhoods including Ravenswood, Rocky Ripple and Broad Ripple, with the White River cresting near record levels.
  • The storm system, which began with a derecho on August 11, left nearly one million utility customers without power across Indiana, Ohio, Illinois and Kentucky.

A Week of Devastation Across Indiana

Powerful storms and flooding have killed at least six people in Indiana since a derecho barreled through the Midwest on August 11, state officials said Saturday, as President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration that will funnel federal resources to more than 50 hard-hit counties.

https://x.com/CBSNews/status/2088771702993953077

The dead include a 4-year-old boy, three females and two males, the Indiana State Emergency Operations Center confirmed. Two deaths occurred in Delaware County, with one each in Jennings, Lake, Porter and LaPorte counties. Authorities are still investigating additional deaths that may be linked to the storm system.

Among the victims was 19-year-old Matthew Morey, a Purdue-bound Delta High School graduate whose body was recovered from the rain-swollen Mississinewa River on Saturday. Morey had gone missing August 12 when he and three friends jumped from a bridge into the river. The body of Stephanie Sallee, a 59-year-old Muncie resident, was found in a cornfield after her car was swept away by floodwaters.

Record-Breaking Flooding Engulfs Indianapolis

The White River, which runs through the heart of Indianapolis, crested at 21.1 feet on Saturday evening — levels not seen in decades. In the Broad Ripple neighborhood, the river surged from 2.4 feet on Tuesday to over 21 feet by Saturday, submerging streets, storefronts and backyards.

"The water is still rising and will be rising all day long. Heed the warnings."

— Todd Wilson, Indianapolis DPW Director

More than 400 residents were evacuated from the Ravenswood neighborhood, with at least 38 people rescued by water rescue teams. The town of Rocky Ripple, built on a spit of land between the White River and the Indiana Central Canal, was effectively sealed off when authorities closed the last floodgate on the 53rd Street Bridge, its only exit.

Noblesville Mayor Chris Jensen described the flooding as "absolutely historic," with water reaching 21 feet in his city. Hamilton County declared a state of emergency as more than 30 roads were closed. In Carmel, residents of an assisted living facility were among roughly 40 people evacuated.

Trump Approves Emergency Declaration

Governor Mike Braun, who declared a statewide disaster emergency on August 13, had requested a presidential emergency declaration through FEMA on August 14. Trump approved it late Saturday, unlocking federal assistance for emergency response costs.

FEMA's declaration covers 53 counties and allows the agency to reimburse 75% of eligible costs, which typically includes rescue operations, emergency sheltering and debris clearance. The move does not yet constitute a full disaster declaration, which could unlock more comprehensive aid for individual residents and businesses.

Indiana Department of Homeland Security executive director Jonathan Whitham compared the damage to the state's devastating June 2008 floods and predicted tens of millions of dollars in property and infrastructure losses.

"I expect this to be a very extensive cleanup and recovery operation, almost statewide."

— Jonathan Whitham, Indiana Department of Homeland Security

Communities Rally Amid Destruction

Even as floodwaters continued rising, communities mobilized. In Broad Ripple, Eric Fox interrupted a bike ride with his sons to deliver sandbags to Rusted Moon Outfitters, where staff fought to keep water from breaching the storefront. The Red Cross set up shelters at the Washington Township Adult Education Center and activated a pet-friendly facility on the west side.

Citizens Energy temporarily paused some operations at its White River North Water Treatment Center but said drinking water remained safe, asking only that residents limit discretionary use.

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita warned residents to watch for scammers posing as FEMA responders, after reports emerged near Cambridge City — a Wayne County town devastated by earlier flooding that saw winds reach 99 mph during the initial derecho.

More Storms on the Horizon

While meteorologists expect the rain to clear around Indianapolis, a storm system over northern Indiana could bring additional rainfall this weekend. The White River is not expected to fall to moderate levels in Marion County until Sunday evening, and officials warned that flooding could spread into areas south of the city along the river.

Governor Braun pointed to Indiana's $1.14 billion rainy day fund as a buffer against future extreme weather, acknowledging that a warming atmosphere is increasing the state's annual precipitation. Indiana has already seen a record 81 confirmed tornadoes in 2026.
nri_angle: The historic flooding across Indiana and the broader Midwest affects Indian Americans and other diaspora communities settled in the region, particularly in the Indianapolis metro area.
